deep.reconstruction:
This page continues Euler's table (n = 9100 to 70000, catchword 75000) for designing water conduits. A reservoir ('castellum') stands at height q above the fountain mouth. It feeds a pipe whose length is n times its diameter. The fountain then rises to v = N q − M feet (§113 on the next page). Recomputing the entries shows they follow N = (4000/n)(1 − e^{−n/4000}) and M = 30(1 − e^{−n/4000}). Checks: n=10000 gives N = 0.4(1−e^{−2.5}) = 0.3672 and M = 30(1−0.0821) = 27.537. n=20000 gives N = 0.19865 and M = 29.7979. n=9000 gives N = 0.3976. Most other entries agree to about 1 unit in the 4th decimal.

The formulas are what Euler's hypothesis gives. He treats fluid friction like solid (Amontons) friction: the drag on the pipe wall is proportional to the absolute pressure on it, atmosphere included. Let p be the absolute pressure head, s the length in diameters, and let the pipe descend uniformly by q over n diameters. Then dp/ds = q/n − p/4000, with p(0) = 30 ft, the water-barometer height Euler uses for the atmosphere. Integrating gives p(n) = 4000(q/n)(1 − e^{−n/4000}) + 30 e^{−n/4000}. Subtracting the 30 ft of atmosphere at the outlet gives v = N q − M with the N and M above.

Hence, as §§113–114 state, for large n (above about 50000) N ≈ 4000/n and M ≈ 30 ft. Friction reduces the ideal height v = q in two ways: q is multiplied by N < 1, and then up to 30 ft is subtracted, an effect Euler attributes to atmospheric pressure. The page is purely numerical tabulation serving this practical hydraulic problem.
errors: n=34000: M printed 29,9973; the formula gives 29.9939 (the printed value also breaks monotonicity).
n=37000: M printed 29,9937; the correct value is 29.9971 (digit transposition; it breaks monotonicity).
n=36000: N printed 1,1111; it should be 0,1111.
n=16000: M printed 29,4404; 30(1−e^{−4}) = 29.4505. This is a computational or printing error, visible as an irregular difference sequence.

Small last-digit computational deviations occur. Examples: M at 9100 (printed 26.9156, computed 26.9163) and at 31000–33000 (printed 29.9874/29.9901/29.9925, computed 29.9871/29.9899/29.9922). N at 9800 (printed 0.3732, computed 0.3729) and at 9900 (printed 0.3702, computed 0.3700).
n=60000: N printed 0,0666 (truncated); it should round to 0,0667.

The model itself is physically wrong for real pipes. Head loss in pipes depends on velocity (roughly velocity squared: Chézy, Prony, Darcy–Weisbach), not on absolute pressure, so the predicted 'atmospheric' loss of up to 30 ft has no physical counterpart.

ideas.what: Closed-form tabulation of fountain height through a long conduit: v = q·(4000/n)(1−e^{−n/4000}) − 30(1−e^{−n/4000}).
ideas.modern_name: Head-loss / jet-height table for pipe flow under a pressure-proportional (Coulomb-type) friction law
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (E260); the friction law is an adaptation of the Amontons–Coulomb solid friction law
ideas.where_published: E260, Novi Commentarii Acad. Petrop. 6 (1761), §§ around 110–114; reprinted in Opera omnia series II (fluid volumes; exact volume unsure)

ideas.what: Fluid friction on pipe walls taken proportional to absolute pressure, including atmospheric pressure, giving exponential decay of pressure along the pipe.
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (E260); discussed in Truesdell's histories of fluid mechanics (exact location unsure)

deep.surprise_reason: A routine numerical table whose entries follow a simple exponential closed form from Euler's own (later abandoned) friction hypothesis. The only findings are a few printing and computational errors; there is no new mathematics or uncredited result.

n=34000 N: '0,1176' (the image digits are smudged).
